headline: Chips still bleeding, all eyes on this morning's CPI print
body: Tuesday's close was more stall than selloff: the S&P 500 eked out a loss of just 0.02% to 7,805.45, the Nasdaq Composite fell a sharper 0.15% to 27,204.38, and the Dow slipped 0.35% to 51,670.10. The drag was concentrated, not broad -- semiconductor and memory names extended their recent slide on fresh worries about AI-spending sustainability and intensifying Chinese competition, with Applied Materials down over 7% and Micron off more than 4%. Bank earnings added a second, more mixed thread: JPMorgan's results missed on both lines even as management raised its net-interest-income guidance, and the financial sector as a whole has shed roughly 4% over the past month -- the second-worst sector showing -- as higher rates squeeze margins even while helping lending income. Together it reads as rotation and digestion within a market still near highs, rather than a broad risk-off turn.

The bigger swing factor sits in rates rather than equities: the 10-year Treasury yield has pushed to its highest levels since the early 2000s amid heavy issuance and sticky inflation, with oil holding above $100 a barrel adding its own upward pressure on price expectations. That makes this morning's September CPI release the day's real catalyst -- consensus looks for a step-up to roughly 3.6% year-over-year from 3.4%, and a hotter-than-expected number would likely pressure both bonds and the rate-sensitive parts of the equity market further, while an in-line or softer print could offer relief to both. Retail-sentiment chatter was thin and inconclusive in today's search results, and recent research suggests forums like WallStreetBets have become more a lagging reaction to price action than a leading signal, so this read leans on price action, yields, and earnings rather than social-sentiment data.
